chunks: Muhammad ibn Isma'il narrated from al-Fadl ibn Shazaan, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Ibrahim ibn Umar, from Amr ibn Shimr, from Jabir, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

The Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'When it is the first day of Shawwal, a caller proclaims: O Believers! Go forth to your awards.' Then he (peace be upon him) said: 'O Jabir! The awards of Allah are not like the awards of these kings.' Then he (peace be upon him) said: 'It is the Day of Awards.'

key_terms.الْمُلُوك: Kings or rulers, representing temporal authority.
key_terms.جَوَائِز: Awards, rewards, or prizes (plural of jawazah).
key_terms.شَوَّال: The tenth month of the Islamic lunar calendar, following Ramadan.
key_terms.يَوْمُ الْجَوَائِز: The Day of Awards, referring to Eid al-Fitr.

ai.seo_question: What is the spiritual significance of the first day of Shawwal according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: In Al-Kafi, Shaykh al-Kulayni records this narration linking the first of Shawwal to a celestial announcement where believers are summoned to receive their 'awards' (jawā'iz), a term emphasizing the gratuitous nature of divine grace rather than earned wages. This tradition underscores the Shia emphasis on Eid al-Fitr as a spiritual milestone where the faithful transition from the discipline of Ramadan to the joy of divine acceptance, contrasting heavenly generosity with the transactional gifts of earthly monarchs. The concept of 'jawā'iz' reflects the theological principle that ultimate success is a gift from Allah, reinforcing the believer's gratitude and hope on this blessed day.
